summary: This unit teaches you to plan and lead housekeeping on electrical jobs, in the workshop and in the store. You will learn to keep work areas, boards and switchrooms clean and clear, leave unfinished work safe, sort and dispose of electrical waste, store materials, tools and chemicals properly, deal with spills and fire risks, and inspect, record and improve housekeeping with a team.

blocks.p: Housekeeping is not 'tidying up at the end'. It is the way a job is organised so that people can work, move and escape safely, equipment stays clean and cool, materials can be found, and waste leaves the site properly. On electrical work it has a special edge: a metal filing in a board, a missing blank, a damp floor or a pile of cardboard against a light fitting can cause a shock or a fire. At Level 3 you plan housekeeping into the job, set the standard for your team, check it and put right what is wrong.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan housekeeping for a job
Decide bins, storage, barriers, cleaning times and who does what before the work starts, and allow time for it every day.
Keep work areas safe while work goes on
Keep walkways, exits, isolators, extinguishers and the space in front of boards clear; control leads, dust, tools at height and offcuts.
Clean electrical equipment safely
Isolate and prove dead, then clean boards, panels and light fittings by dry methods with the right tools and products.
Leave unfinished work safe
Make cable ends safe, fit covers and blanks, cover holes, lock away tools and materials, and tell the person in charge what is off.
Sort and dispose of waste
Separate copper scrap, packaging, PVC, lamps and tubes, batteries and e-waste, and send each the right way. Never burn cable.
Store materials, tools and chemicals
Rack, label and protect cable, conduit, fittings, ladders, instruments, chemicals and batteries.
Deal with spills, leaks and fire risks
Use the spill kit and the SDS, keep water and electricity apart, and remove fuel from sources of heat.
Inspect, record and improve
Use a checklist, score it, give each fault an owner and a date, find the cause of repeat problems, and lead the team by example.

head: Person
Responsibility
rows: Every worker and trainee
Keeps their own work area safe and tidy all the time: 'clean as you go'.
Team leader (you, at Level 3)
Plans the housekeeping, provides bins and storage, checks during the day, makes safe at the end, and corrects poor practice.
Supervisor or instructor
Sets the rules, provides the resources, inspects, and acts on reports.
Client or building manager
Tells you the site rules, the waste arrangements, and who must be told when circuits are off.

blocks.note: Jamaica's workplace safety laws and the Centre's rules expect workplaces to be kept clean, with clear passages and safe access. On a client's premises you also follow the client's rules. When rules differ, follow the stricter one.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, then try the practice test and read every explanation. Many answers depend on judgement: what to do first, and what matters most. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own checklists, waste containers and store.

sections.title: Why housekeeping matters, and planning it

head: Poor housekeeping
What it leads to
rows: Offcuts, stripped insulation, screws and conduit ends on the floor
Slips, trips and falls: stripped insulation rolls underfoot like marbles.
Trailing leads and hoses
Trips; leads crushed or cut so that live conductors show.
Filings, wire strands and offcuts left inside boards
Short circuits, tracking, arcing and fire when the board is energised.
Open boards, missing blanks, exposed cable ends
Electric shock to workers, cleaners, children and other occupants.
Dust, paper and packaging near boards, lights and heaters
Fire; overheating of equipment whose vents are blocked.
Blocked walkways, exits, isolators and extinguishers
Slow escape and slow response in an emergency.
Tools left on ladders, in ceilings and inside equipment
Falling objects; lost tools; a spanner across live busbars.
Materials dumped anywhere
Damage, loss, theft, wasted time searching and buying twice.
Waste mixed together or burned
Toxic smoke, mercury and acid released, fines, and an angry client.

blocks.p: Good housekeeping also saves time and money, and it is the part of your work the client sees. A neat, safe site tells the client that the wiring behind the wall was done with the same care.
**5S** is a workplace organisation method used in many industries. Its five steps give you a plan for a store, a workshop or a site cabin.

head: Step
Meaning
Electrical example
rows: 1. Sort
Remove what is not needed.
Clear out dead stock, broken tools, empty reels and scrap from the store.
2. Set in order
A place for everything, and everything in its place.
Labelled bins for each size of connector; a shadow board for hand tools; racks for conduit.
3. Shine
Clean, and inspect while you clean.
Vacuum the bays; while cleaning, spot a cracked outlet or a frayed lead.
4. Standardise
Make the good way the normal way for everyone.
The same colour-coded waste bins and the same daily checklist in every bay.
5. Sustain
Keep it going.
Weekly inspections, scores on the notice board, toolbox talks, leading by example.

blocks.p: Housekeeping that is not planned does not happen. Before the job starts, decide:

ul: **Where** materials, tools and ladders will be kept during the day and locked away at night.
**Which waste** the job will make, and a labelled container for each kind: copper scrap, recycling, general waste, hazardous waste.
**How** dust and noise will be controlled, and when the dustiest work will be done.
**What barriers and signs** are needed to keep other people out of the work area.
**When** cleaning happens: as you go, at each break, and a set time before the end of the day (often the last 20 to 30 minutes).
**Who** does what, including who makes the electrical work safe and who does the final check.
**Who must be told** each day what is off and what is safe to use.

flow: Plan bins, storage, barriers and times
Brief the team: the standard and each person's area
Clean as you go
Check at each break
Make safe and clean at the end of the day
Inspect, record and put right

blocks.note: **Clean as you go** means clearing waste and returning tools while you work, not leaving it all to the end. Put a bag or bucket beside you for offcuts and stripped insulation before you start to strip cable.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Keeping the work area safe while you work

ul: Keep walkways, stairs, corridors and exits clear at all times. They are escape routes. Cable drums, ladders, boxes and reels do not belong in them; drums can also roll.
Never block an **isolator**, emergency stop, distribution board, fire extinguisher, fire alarm call point, first-aid kit or eyewash station. In an emergency, seconds count.
Report failed lights in work areas, stores and corridors. Poor light causes mistakes and accidents, and hides hazards.

blocks.h: The working space in front of electrical equipment

blocks.p: The NEC requires a clear **working space** in front of panels, switchboards and other equipment that may need to be worked on while live. For the ordinary 110/220 V boards found in most Jamaican buildings, that space is at least about **0.9 m (3 ft) deep**, at least **0.75 m (30 in) wide** or the width of the equipment if that is greater, and about **2 m (6.5 ft) high**. It must never be used for storage. Larger and higher-voltage equipment needs more space: follow the drawings and the code.

blocks.note: A switchroom is not a store. Boxes, drums, ladders, mops and paint tins in front of a switchboard stop a person working safely, block their escape from an arc flash, feed a fire, and block ventilation. If you find a switchroom used as a store, report it and have it cleared.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Take temporary power only from a point protected by a suitable breaker and by **GFCI (RCD)** protection, as the Centre's or the site's rules say.
Inspect every lead before use: sheath, plug, socket and cord grips. Tag out and report a damaged lead; do not tape it.

Route leads along walls or overhead on hooks, not across walkways or through doorways where doors and trolleys crush them. Where a lead must cross a route, protect it with a cable cover or ramp rated for the traffic.
**Fully unwind a cable reel** before running a heavy load. A coiled lead cannot lose its heat and can melt.
Do not overload adaptors or plug one extension lead into another.
Keep leads and connectors out of water and off wet ground.
At the end of the day unplug, coil loosely, check and store leads dry. Switch off and make safe the temporary supply.

blocks.h: Tools, ladders and work at height

ul: Do not leave tools on top of ladders, on ledges or in ceiling spaces: they fall on people, or they are left behind.
Use a tool belt, pouch or lanyard at height, and a bucket or bag on a line to raise and lower tools.
Count tools into and out of ceiling voids, panels and machines.
Do not leave a ladder standing unattended where children or the public can climb it. Take it down, or lock it away.

blocks.p: Chasing walls and drilling concrete or block make fine dust that harms the lungs, spreads through a building and settles inside electrical equipment. Control it at the source.

head: Control
How
rows: Extraction on the tool
Use a chaser or drill with a dust shroud connected to a vacuum made for fine dust.
Contain the area
Close doors, seal gaps with plastic sheet and tape, cover nearby equipment and furniture, and cover or close boards that are not being worked on.
Timing
Do the dustiest and noisiest work when the building is empty, or when the people next door agree.
Clean-up
Vacuum; do not dry-sweep, which throws the fine dust back into the air. Never blow it away with compressed air.
PPE
Dust masks of the right type, eye protection and hearing protection for the people doing the work.

ul: Mark off the work area with barriers, tape or cones and warning signs: an **exclusion zone** that keeps other people out.
Keep everything inside the zone: tools, materials, leads, ladders and waste.
Agree with the person in charge when circuits can be switched off, when noisy or dusty work can be done, and where waste goes. Do not use the client's bins unless they agree.
Protect floors and furniture with dust sheets. Clean as you go, and leave the place at least as clean as you found it.
Take extra care in schools, clinics and homes: children and patients do not read warning signs.
Do not use a wet mop, hose or bucket of water near open boards, floor outlets, extension leads or equipment. Water near live parts can give a shock.
Use a vacuum or a slightly damp cloth on surfaces well away from live parts, and dry methods near them.
If cleaners will work in the area after you, leave no open boxes, loose ends or floor boxes without covers.

blocks.p: Dust, insects, moisture and metal particles inside electrical equipment cause overheating, tracking (current creeping across a dirty surface), short circuits and corrosion. Cleaning is part of installation and of maintenance, but it must be done **dead**.

flow: Agree the shutdown with the person in charge
Isolate the board at its supply; lock off and tag
Prove dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after
Find any parts that stay live, such as incoming terminals fed from elsewhere, and keep clear or isolate upstream
Remove covers; inspect for filings, offcuts, dust, damp, insects and nests, and signs of overheating
Vacuum with a non-metallic nozzle and a soft brush
Check that no tools, screws or offcuts are left inside; count your tools
Refit all covers, barriers and blanks
Record the work; the authorised person re-energises

head: Method
Use it?
Why
rows: Vacuum cleaner with a non-metallic (plastic) nozzle and a soft brush
Yes
It removes the dust instead of moving it. A plastic nozzle cannot bridge terminals or scratch insulation.
Compressed air or a blower
No, unless the maker's procedure says so
It drives dust and filings deeper into breakers, contactors and vents, and into the air you breathe.
Wet cloth, water or general-purpose spray
No
Moisture and residues cause tracking and corrosion.
Wire brush, metal scraper
No
It sheds metal and damages surfaces and insulation.
Lint-free cloth with an approved electrical cleaner
Only as the maker and the SDS allow
For contacts and insulators, on isolated equipment, with ventilation; let it evaporate fully before energising.

blocks.note: **The line side of a main switch stays live when the switch is off.** Switching off a panel's own main isolator does not make its incoming terminals dead. To clean near them, isolate at the upstream breaker or switch, lock it off and prove dead at the panel.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Drilling or punching a hole in a board, trunking or panel makes metal filings (swarf). A single filing across two terminals, or between a live part and the case, can cause a short circuit or tracking the moment the board is switched on. Wherever you can, remove the gland plate and drill it away from the board. Otherwise cover the equipment below the hole before you drill, catch the filings, and vacuum afterwards. Check again before switch-on.

In Jamaica, ants, wasps, lizards, cockroaches and rats often get into boards, meter cabinets, outdoor panels and pump controls through open knockouts and unsealed conduit entries. Nests hold moisture, block vents and bridge live parts; rats chew insulation. Remove nests only with the equipment isolated and proved dead. Then close the way in: fit blanks, bushings and gland plates, and seal unused entries with the proper fittings.

ul: Read the label and the **safety data sheet (SDS)** before using any product.

Contact cleaner, isopropyl alcohol and many solvents are **flammable**. Use them only on isolated equipment, away from sparks and heat, with good ventilation, and let them evaporate completely before the supply is restored.
Sprays on live equipment can ignite, cause tracking or carry current back to you.
Wear the PPE the SDS gives, usually gloves and eye protection. Never mix products.
Use only cleaners the equipment's maker allows: some solvents attack plastics, labels and insulation.

blocks.p: Dust and dead insects on lamps, diffusers and reflectors cut the light output and trap heat, which shortens the life of lamps and drivers. Clean fittings when they are relamped, with the circuit isolated. Wipe diffusers and reflectors with a soft cloth, slightly damp if the maker allows, and let them dry before refitting. Measuring the light level before and after shows the client what cleaning has gained.
**Example.** A classroom reads 320 lux before the fittings are cleaned and 400 lux after. The gain is 80 lux; 80 ÷ 320 × 100 = **25%** more light for no extra energy.

ul: Wipe instruments clean and check the leads, probes and clips for damage at the end of each day.
Return each instrument to its case with its leads. Store it in a dry cupboard, away from heat and knocks.
Remove batteries from instruments that will be stored for a long time, so that they cannot leak.
Report damage and overdue calibration. An instrument that reads wrongly is worse than none.

sections.title: Leaving work safe at the end of the day

blocks.p: An unfinished installation is at its most dangerous when the electrician is not there. Cleaners, security guards, children and the client's staff do not know what is live. Plan to stop about half an hour early, and deal with the **electrical hazards first**, then the tidying.

flow: Stop work in time: about 30 minutes before you leave
Make every circuit you worked on safe: isolated, locked off and tagged, or its ends made safe
Fit covers, lids and blanking plates; close and lock boards
Cover or barrier holes in floors and ceilings, with a warning sign
Take down ladders; remove or lock away tools, leads and materials
Bag waste and take it to the right containers; vacuum dust
Check that the circuits the client needs are working
Tell the person in charge what is off and what is safe to use
Write it in the job diary or handover note

head: Situation
How to leave it
rows: New cables pulled in but not yet connected
Leave them **disconnected at the supply end**. Insulate each conductor end with an insulated cap, connector or end cap, coil the cable neatly, and tie it up out of reach.
A circuit being altered
Keep it isolated, locked off and tagged at the board. Insulate any exposed ends as well, in case someone removes the isolation.
An outlet or switch removed for decorating or repair
Isolate the circuit, or terminate the conductors in a proper connector inside a box with a blank cover. Never leave bare copper, even 'dead'.
Cables pushed into a ceiling or wall for later
Not acceptable unless the ends are capped, the cable is labelled and it is recorded. Unmarked cable ends in a ceiling are a trap for the next person.

blocks.note: Insulating tape alone is not a safe end. It unwinds in the heat and falls off. Use an insulated cap, a twist-on or lever connector of the right size, or a terminal block inside an enclosure.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Where a breaker has been removed or a way is unused, fit the board maker's **blanking plate** (filler plate) so that no one can touch live parts through the gap. Cardboard and tape are not blanks: they fall out, they burn, and a finger goes straight through them.
Refit every cover, lid and faceplate with all its screws. A cover held by one screw is not secure.
Close unused knockouts and conduit entries with the proper plugs.
Cover holes in floors with a fixed cover strong enough to stand on, marked as a cover; barrier and sign openings in ceilings and walls.
Lock away cable, copper offcuts, breakers and tools every night. Copper has a ready resale value and is a common target for theft.
Locking up also stops other people using your tools, ladders and leads unsafely.
Protect open work from rain: afternoon showers are common, and water in a board or conduit means delay and danger. Cover roof and wall openings, and close outdoor enclosures.
In the hurricane season, secure loose materials and follow the site's storm plan.

blocks.p: Before you leave, tell the client, building manager or supervisor, in plain words: which circuits or rooms are off; what is safe to use; what must not be touched; where barriers are and why; and when you will be back. Give your phone number. Then note the same points in the job diary. A two-minute handover prevents the caretaker 'helpfully' switching a breaker back on.

Think of waste in this order: **reduce** it (accurate ordering, careful cutting), **reuse** what you can (useful offcuts, drums), **recycle** what has value (copper, cardboard), and **dispose** of the rest properly. Set up labelled containers before the job starts, and never leave waste on the client's premises unless that has been agreed.

head: Waste
Hazard or value
What to do
rows: Copper offcuts, stripped wire, old cable, brass and aluminium
Resale value; a target for theft
Keep in a secure, labelled container. Weigh it and record it. Sell it only through the firm's or the Centre's procedure, to a licensed dealer.
Useful lengths of cable and conduit
Still good material
Coil, tie and label with size and length; return to the store.
Short PVC conduit ends, cable sheath, stripped insulation
Burning gives off toxic, corrosive fumes
General waste or the plastics bin. **Never burn.**
Cardboard, paper and plastic packaging
Fire fuel; trip hazard
Flatten and bag as the work goes; recycle where there is a collection.
Fluorescent tubes, compact fluorescent and discharge lamps
Contain **mercury**; sharp glass
Keep whole, in their boxes or a tube container. Hazardous waste: special collection.
LED lamps and drivers, electronic ballasts, meters, circuit boards
**E-waste**: contain metals and other harmful materials
Keep apart for e-waste collection.
Very old ballasts and capacitors that leak oil
May contain PCBs, a toxic oil
Do not handle with bare hands. Bag, label and report for specialist disposal.
Lead-acid batteries (standby, UPS, alarm, solar)
Lead and sulphuric acid
Keep upright with the terminals covered; return to the supplier or a licensed recycler.
Lithium and other small batteries
Fire if shorted or damaged
Tape the terminals; keep in a separate container for battery recycling.
Solvent tins, aerosol cans, oily or solvent-soaked rags
Flammable; pressurised
As the label and SDS say. Rags in a closed metal bin. Never burn or puncture cans.
Plaster, block dust and rubble from chasing
Dust; weight
Bag and seal it; take it to the skip or the agreed disposal point.

blocks.note: **Never burn cable to get the copper.** Burning PVC gives off hydrogen chloride and other poisonous, corrosive fumes that harm the lungs and damage nearby equipment. Open burning of waste is also against Jamaica's environmental rules. Copper is sold as cable scrap, or stripped mechanically.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Stop work and move people away; keep them from walking through the glass
Open windows and doors; switch off fans and air-conditioning that would spread the vapour
Let the room air for at least 10 to 15 minutes, or as the Centre's procedure says
Wearing gloves, scoop up glass and powder with stiff card; pick up small pieces with sticky tape
Wipe the area with a damp paper towel
Seal everything used, including the card, tape, towel and gloves, in a bag or jar; label it
Store it with the hazardous lamp waste; wash your hands; report it

blocks.p: Do **not** use a vacuum cleaner or a broom on a broken tube: they spread the mercury-bearing powder into the air and contaminate the machine.

Plan waste collection before the containers overflow. **Example:** a skip holds 6 m³ and the job makes about 0.8 m³ of waste a day. 6 ÷ 0.8 = 7.5, so the skip is full during day 8: book the exchange for the end of day 7. Record copper scrap by weight: 26.5 kg at a made-up price of J$850 per kg is 26.5 × 850 = **J$22 525**, which belongs to the firm or the client, not to whoever carries it away.

blocks.note: The National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA) manages ordinary solid waste in Jamaica, and the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) deals with hazardous waste and pollution. Collection routes for tubes, batteries and e-waste change, so follow the Centre's or the firm's current arrangement and use licensed collectors.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Storing materials, tools, chemicals and batteries

blocks.p: A good store lets anyone find the right item quickly, keeps materials in good condition, and keeps people safe. Heavy items go low, things used often go where they are easy to reach, and nothing is stored in front of boards, isolators, extinguishers or exits.

head: Item
How to store it
Why
rows: Cable drums
On chocks, in a drum bay or on a drum rack; heavy drums at ground level; under cover
Drums roll and crush; sun and rain damage the sheath and let water into cut ends.
Part-used coils and rolls
Coiled, tied, labelled with size, type and length; on racks or hooks
The right cable is found quickly and stock is known; loose cable tangles and kinks.
Conduit and trunking
Flat on racks, supported along the length; never leaning against a wall or lying in a walkway
Leaning lengths fall and bend; PVC bows in the heat.
Fittings and accessories
In labelled bins by size, type and rating; heavy boxes on low shelves
No mixing of sizes; quick stock checks; no lifting injuries.
Breakers, drivers, electronic parts
In their boxes; dry, clean and secure
Dust, damp and knocks damage them; they are costly and easily stolen.
Ladders and steps
Flat on wall brackets or racks, out of sun and rain; secured
Sunlight weakens fibreglass, and damp rots or corrodes; a leaning ladder falls or is 'borrowed'.
Hand tools
On a shadow board or in marked drawers
A gap on the board shows at once that a tool is missing.
Test instruments
In their cases, in a dry, locked cupboard
Damp, heat and knocks affect accuracy and safety.
Extension leads
Coiled loosely on hooks, after inspection
Tight coils and kinks damage the conductors.

ul: Keep chemicals in their **original, labelled containers**, tightly closed. Never decant them into drink bottles or unmarked jars: someone will drink from one.
Store flammable products (contact cleaner, isopropyl alcohol, solvent cement, some paints) in a ventilated flammables cabinet, away from heat, sparks and sunlight.
Keep only what is needed, and keep the SDS for every product where workers can read it.
Keep the spill kit near the chemicals and the batteries, and know where the eyewash is.

Lead-acid batteries on charge give off **hydrogen**, a gas that burns and can explode. Charge them only in a ventilated place, with no smoking, sparks or naked flames. Switch the charger off before connecting or disconnecting the clips.
Store batteries upright, off the bare floor, with their terminals covered so that a dropped tool cannot short them.
Keep acid neutraliser (such as sodium bicarbonate, where the SDS allows it), gloves, goggles and an apron near the batteries.
Keep lithium batteries cool and away from metal objects. Remove swollen or damaged ones from use at once.

blocks.note: Nothing is stored in a switchroom, in a battery room that is not designed for it, or in the working space in front of any board. If the store is short of space, the answer is to sort and remove what is not needed, not to use the switchroom.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: How housekeeping prevents fire and shock

blocks.p: A fire needs fuel, heat and air. Electrical work brings the heat: overheated leads, lamps, drivers, loose connections, soldering irons and sparks from cutting. Housekeeping removes the fuel and keeps the heat under control.

head: Hazard
Housekeeping control
rows: Dust, paper, cardboard, rags and offcuts near boards, lights, heaters and motors
Clear them away every day; keep vents open; keep stores of packaging away from equipment.
Coiled reels and overloaded adaptors
Unwind reels fully; one heavy load per outlet; inspect leads.
Filings and offcuts inside boards
Clean and inspect before switch-on.
Solvent vapour
Ventilate; no ignition sources; lids on; rags in a closed metal bin.
Damaged plugs, outlets and covers
Tag out, report and replace.
Water near electrical equipment
Dry cleaning methods; report leaks; keep equipment off wet floors.
Hot work (grinding, soldering, heat guns)
Clear the area of anything that burns; have an extinguisher at hand; check the area again after the work.

ul: For fires in electrical equipment use **carbon dioxide (CO2)** or dry powder (dry chemical). On US-type extinguishers, look for Class C.
**Never use water or foam on live equipment**: water conducts, and the current can travel back up the stream to you.
Keep extinguishers on their brackets, in date, visible and never blocked. Check them on your inspection.
Fight a fire only if it is small, you are trained and your escape route is behind you. Otherwise raise the alarm, get out and call 110.

head: Spill
What to do
rows: Battery acid (sulphuric acid)

Keep people away. Wear goggles, acid-resistant gloves and an apron. Contain it with the spill kit. Neutralise it as the SDS says, for example with sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) until the fizzing stops, then absorb it and dispose of it as hazardous waste. Do not wash it into a drain. Report it.
Solvent or contact cleaner
Remove sources of ignition, ventilate, absorb with the spill kit, bag the waste and dispose of it as the SDS says.
Oil
Absorb with granules or pads; clean the floor so that it is not slippery; dispose of the waste properly.
Water
Find and stop the source if it is safe; keep it away from electrical equipment; dry the floor; put out a warning sign.

blocks.note: Acid on the skin or in the eyes: rinse with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 to 20 minutes and get medical help. Know where the eyewash and the nearest tap are before you work near batteries.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Roof leaks, burst pipes and flooding are common after heavy rain. If water is dripping onto or near a board, panel or machine:

flow: Keep people away from the area
Do not touch the wet equipment
Isolate it from a dry, safe point upstream, if you can do so safely
Report it at once
Have the equipment inspected, dried and tested before it is switched on again

blocks.p: Wiping a live board dry, or standing a bucket on top of it, puts you in contact with wet, possibly live metal. A metal cover does not make a wet board safe.

sections.title: Inspecting, recording and leading the team

blocks.p: An inspection compares the workplace with a written standard. Do a quick walk-round every day and a formal checklist inspection at set times, often weekly. During an inspection, **do not open boards or remove covers**: you are looking, not working.

head: Checklist item
Why it is on the list
rows: All board and box covers fitted; blanks in every unused way
No live parts can be touched.
Clear working space in front of boards; isolators labelled and not blocked
Safe work and a fast shutdown in an emergency.
Walkways and exits clear; floors free of offcuts, insulation and screws
No slips or trips; a clear escape route.
Leads undamaged, not trailing, reels unwound; outlets and plugs undamaged
No shock, fire or trips.
Tools on the shadow board and counted; instruments in their cases
No lost tools, no tools left inside equipment, accurate instruments.
Materials racked and labelled; drums chocked; ladders on brackets
Nothing falls or rolls; stock is found and protected.
Waste in the right containers; copper secured; tubes whole; no waste near heat
Safe disposal, recycling and fire prevention.
Chemicals closed, labelled and in the cabinet; SDS available; spill kit complete
No fire, poisoning or spill left untreated.
Extinguishers in place and in date; lighting working
A fast response; faults are seen.

blocks.p: Mark each item OK or not OK. The score is the number OK ÷ the number checked × 100. **Example:** 42 items checked, 36 OK: 36 ÷ 42 × 100 = **85.7%**, say 86%. A score lets you compare weeks and bays, but the action list is what improves things.

head: Fault found
Action
Owner
By when
Status
rows: Cracked outlet cover, bay 3
Tag out of use; replace the cover
T. Williams
Today
Open
Conduit leaning in the corner of the store
Rack it; mark the rack by size
Store team
Friday
Open
Failed light over bench 2
Report to maintenance; replace the lamp
Team leader
Tomorrow
Open

ul: Every fault gets an **owner and a date**. A fault with no owner stays a fault.
Make dangerous items safe at once: tag out a damaged outlet or lead before you write it down.
At the next inspection, check first that the last list was completed.

blocks.h: When the same fault keeps coming back

blocks.p: If the same bench is untidy every week, tidying it again changes nothing. Ask why, with the people who use it. Is there nowhere to put the tools? Is the bin too far away? Is there too little time at the end of the session? Does nobody feel it is theirs? Agree a fix that removes the cause: a shadow board, a nearer bin, five minutes set aside, a named person. Then check whether it worked.

ul: **Explain why** at the start: on an electrical job, housekeeping prevents trips, cuts, shocks and fires, and it is the quality the client sees.
**Plan it in**: bins, bags and storage ready, time allowed at every break and at the end of the day, and each person given an area.
**Lead by example.** If you step over the offcuts, so will everyone else.
**Check at set times** with a short checklist, and praise good work.
**Correct on the spot.** If a trainee leaves stripped insulation on the floor, explain the slip risk and have them clear it themselves, as they go. Doing it for them teaches nothing.

**Deal with repeated poor practice fairly**: speak to the person in private, find out if there is a reason, explain the risk, agree what you expect, and check more often. If it does not improve, record it and report it to the supervisor.

blocks.h: The last check before locking up

flow: Machines and equipment off; isolators set as the Centre's rules say
Soldering irons, heaters and chargers off or made safe
Boards closed; training bays made safe
Tools and instruments returned and counted
Waste removed; floors clear
Chemicals put away; cabinets closed
Windows and stores secured; lights off as required; doors locked

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain how poor housekeeping on electrical work leads to shock, fire, falls and loss.
I can plan the housekeeping for a job: bins, storage, barriers, cleaning times and who does what.
I can name the five steps of 5S and give an electrical example of each.
I can keep walkways, exits, isolators, extinguishers and the working space in front of boards clear, and say why.
I can set up, use and clear away leads and temporary supplies safely.
I can control dust from chasing and drilling, and work considerately in an occupied building.
I can clean an isolated board or panel with a vacuum and non-metallic nozzle, and explain why compressed air and wet cloths are not used.
I can explain why the incoming terminals of a board may still be live, and what to do about it.
I can use and store cleaning chemicals as the label and SDS say.
I can leave unfinished work safe: cable ends, blanks, covers, holes, tools and materials.
I can tell the person in charge what is off and what is safe to use, and record it.
I can sort electrical waste and say where each kind goes, and why cable is never burned.
I can clean up a broken fluorescent tube safely.
I can store cable, conduit, fittings, ladders, instruments, chemicals and batteries correctly.
I can deal with a battery acid spill and a leak near a board.
I can run a housekeeping inspection, work out the score and write an action list with owners and dates.
I can find the cause of a repeated housekeeping fault and lead a team to keep up the standard.

What it is

terms: 5S
A workplace organisation method: sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain.
Action list
The list of faults from an inspection, each with an action, an owner and a date.
Blanking plate
A plate fitted in a board cover to close the gap where there is no breaker; also called a blank or filler plate.
Clean as you go
Clearing waste and putting tools away while the work goes on, not at the end.
E-waste
Waste electrical and electronic items such as drivers, meters and circuit boards, which need special collection.
End cap
An insulated cap or connector put on a conductor end to make it safe until it is connected.
Exclusion zone
An area marked off with barriers and signs to keep other people out of the work.
Hazardous waste
Waste that can harm people or the environment, such as tubes, batteries and solvents.
Hydrogen
The flammable gas given off by lead-acid batteries on charge.
Mercury
The toxic metal in fluorescent tubes and some other lamps.
Neutraliser
A substance, such as sodium bicarbonate, used to make spilt acid harmless, where the SDS allows it.
Safety data sheet (SDS)
The supplier's sheet giving a chemical's hazards, storage, PPE, first aid and spill action.
Shadow board
A tool board with the outline of each tool, so that a missing tool is seen at once.
Swarf
Metal filings and chips made by drilling and cutting.
Tracking
Current creeping across a dirty or damp insulating surface, which can lead to a fault or fire.
Working space
The clear space that must be kept in front of electrical equipment for safe work and escape.

c1.title: Rewiring classrooms at a primary school in Ewarton
c1.text: Kemar Lawrence, a Level 3 electrician, leads two trainees rewiring two classrooms at a primary school in Ewarton, St Catherine, while lessons go on in the rooms next door. The job needs block walls chased for new outlet boxes. At 3:30 p.m. on the first day, with 30 minutes left, the state of the job is this: new cables are pulled to the board but not connected, with bare ends; two ways in the board have no breakers and no blanks; offcuts and packaging cover the classroom floor; and two ladders and a cable reel are standing in the corridor that the children use.

c2.title: Cleaning a pump-house control panel near Lionel Town
c2.text: Simone Bailey, a Level 3 technician, is sent with a trainee to clean and inspect the motor control panel in an irrigation pump house on a farm near Lionel Town, Clarendon. Inside the panel are thick dust, an old wasp nest and metal filings from a gland hole drilled last month. The panel's main isolator is on its door; the cable feeding it comes from a breaker in the farm's main switchroom, 60 m away. In that switchroom, bags of fertiliser are stacked against the front of the main switchboard. The trainee has brought an air blower and a can of contact cleaner.

c3.title: Relamping a supermarket in Brown's Town
c3.text: A team led by Level 3 trainee Andre Whyte is replacing 60 old fluorescent tubes with LED tubes in a supermarket in Brown's Town, St Ann, before opening time. The old magnetic ballasts are being removed, and one of them is leaking a dark oily liquid. A light meter at one aisle reads 380 lux before the dusty diffusers are cleaned and 475 lux after. During the work a trainee drops an old tube, which breaks on the floor of the aisle; the clean-up is done with card, tape and gloves.

c4.title: The weekly inspection at a training centre in Black River
c4.text: Sasha-Gaye Thompson, a Level 3 trainee, runs the weekly housekeeping inspection of the electrical workshop and store at a training centre in Black River, St Elizabeth. Her checklist has 64 items, and 56 are OK. Among the faults: isopropyl alcohol kept in an unlabelled water bottle on a bench; the extract fan in the battery charging corner is not running while two lead-acid batteries are on charge; and bench 4 is cluttered with tools and offcuts for the third week running. Last week's action list simply said 'tidy bench 4'.

c5.title: A housing scheme site near Yallahs
c5.text: Jermaine Ellis, a Level 3 electrician, runs the electrical work on a housing scheme near Yallahs, St Thomas. The site's 8 m³ skip was emptied this morning, and the trades fill about 1.25 m³ of it each day. A labourer offers to burn the pile of cable offcuts behind the cabin 'to get the copper out'. The team's extension leads run from the temporary supply across the site road used by delivery trucks.

questions.q: With only 30 minutes left, what should Kemar's team deal with first?
o: Sweeping up the offcuts and packaging in the classroom
The bare cable ends and the open ways in the board
Carrying the ladders and the cable reel out to the van
Writing up the day's progress in the job diary
questions.why: Deal with the hazards that can kill first. Bare ends and gaps in a board can give a child or a cleaner a shock, so the ends are made safe and the board is blanked and closed before the tidying. All four jobs must be done, but in order of risk.

questions.q: A trainee offers to tape pieces of cardboard over the two empty ways in the board until tomorrow. Why is this not acceptable?
o: Cardboard makes the board look untidy to the principal
Tape leaves marks on the paint of the board's cover
The board's maker does not allow any cover to be fitted
It can fall off, burn, or be pushed in by a finger
questions.why: A blank must keep fingers and objects away from live parts and stay in place. Cardboard and tape do neither, and they are fuel inside a board. Fit the board maker's blanking plates, or keep the board isolated and locked.

questions.q: What is the best way to plan the wall chasing in this school?
o: Chase during lessons, with the classroom doors kept shut
Chase at lunch time and sweep the dust up afterwards
Agree a time when the block is empty, and use extraction
Chase quickly in one go so that the dust is over sooner
questions.why: Chasing is the dustiest, noisiest part of the job. In an occupied school the best control is to agree with the principal a time when the children are not there, and still control the dust at the tool with extraction and a vacuum. Dry sweeping only throws fine dust back into the air.

questions.q: What should be done with the ladders and the cable reel in the corridor before the team leaves?
o: Lay them flat along the corridor wall, out of the way
Stand them in a corner with a 'keep off' sign on them
Leave them there, since work starts early the next day
Remove them to a locked room or the van for the night
questions.why: The corridor is the children's escape route, and children will climb a ladder and play with a reel. Anything left there is a trip and fall hazard and may be used unsafely. Take equipment away or lock it up every night.

questions.q: Simone switches off the isolator on the panel door. Which parts inside the panel may still be live?
o: The incoming cable and the isolator's supply-side terminals
The motor terminals and the cable going out to the pump
The overload relay and the contactor's load terminals
None, because the door isolator disconnects the whole panel
questions.why: An isolator makes dead only what is on its load side. The incoming cable and the terminals it lands on stay live until the upstream breaker in the main switchroom is opened and locked off. Prove dead at the panel before any cleaning near those terminals.

questions.q: The trainee wants to blow the dust and filings out of the panel with the air blower. What should Simone tell him?
o: Use the blower, but only on its lowest setting
Use the blower after the contact cleaner has dried
Use a vacuum with a plastic nozzle and a soft brush
Use a wire brush first, then blow the dust away
questions.why: Blowing drives dust and metal filings deeper into contactors, breakers and vents, where a filing can cause a short circuit at switch-on. A vacuum takes the dirt away, and a non-metallic nozzle cannot bridge terminals or damage insulation.

questions.q: How should the contact cleaner be used on the contactor's contacts?
o: Sparingly on the isolated panel, with the door open, left to dry fully
With the panel live, so the contacts can be seen working as they are cleaned
Sprayed generously over every part, then the panel is closed up at once
Mixed with a little water first, to cut the risk of fire from the spray
questions.why: Contact cleaners are usually flammable. Use only what is needed, on dead equipment, with ventilation, and let it evaporate completely before the supply is restored. Spraying live parts risks fire, tracking and shock, and chemicals are never mixed or watered down.

questions.q: After the panel is cleaned, the trainee's tool roll has one empty pocket where a small screwdriver should be. What must happen before the panel is handed back?
o: Hand it back, and look for the screwdriver in the van later
Find the screwdriver; search the panel before it is energised
Hand it back with a note that a screwdriver may be inside
Energise the panel briefly to see whether anything is wrong
questions.why: A tool left inside a panel can bridge live parts and cause an arc flash when the supply is restored. Counting tools in and out is part of the job; if one is missing, the equipment stays isolated until it is found.

questions.q: What should Simone do about the fertiliser bags stacked against the main switchboard?
o: Leave them, as long as the switchboard doors can still open
Restack them neatly so that they take up less of the room
Report it and have the working space in front cleared
Move them to stand behind the switchboard instead
questions.why: The space in front of a switchboard, about 0.9 m deep or more, must be kept clear so that a person can work and escape safely. Stored goods there also feed a fire and block ventilation, and fertiliser dust is corrosive. A switchroom is not a store, front or back.

questions.q: By what percentage did cleaning the diffusers raise the light level in the aisle?
questions.why: The gain is 475 − 380 = 95 lux. As a percentage of the starting level: 95 ÷ 380 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the new level (475) gives 20%, which is the wrong base.

questions.q: What should be done with the card, tape and gloves used to clean up the broken tube?
o: Put them in the supermarket's general waste bin
Seal them in the bag with the broken tube waste
Shake them off outside and reuse them next time
Rinse them at the sink and return them to the van
questions.why: Everything that touched the powder may carry mercury. It is sealed in a labelled bag or jar with the broken glass and stored with the hazardous lamp waste. Rinsing or shaking only spreads the contamination.

questions.q: How should the 59 unbroken old tubes be kept until they are collected?
o: Whole, in the cartons from the new tubes, labelled, in a secure dry place
Crushed into a drum with a lid, so that they take up much less room
Tied in a bundle and stood upright in the corner of the stockroom
Laid loose in the skip, on top of the cardboard so they do not break
questions.why: Fluorescent tubes contain mercury and are hazardous waste while whole or broken. Kept whole in boxes, labelled and out of harm's way, they can go for special collection. Crushing them releases the mercury vapour.

questions.q: How should Andre deal with the ballast that is leaking a dark oily liquid?
o: Wipe it clean with a rag and put it with the scrap metal
Bag and label it without bare-hand contact, and report it
Put it in the general bin, wrapped in plenty of cardboard
Strip it for its copper winding before it is thrown away
questions.why: Very old ballasts and capacitors may contain PCBs, a toxic oil that passes through the skin. Do not touch the liquid: bag and label the ballast and report it for specialist disposal. Sound ballasts go for e-waste or metal recycling as the firm arranges.

questions.q: What is this week's housekeeping score?
questions.why: Score = number OK ÷ number checked × 100 = 56 ÷ 64 × 100 = 87.5%. The figure of 12.5% is the share that failed, not the score.

questions.q: What should Sasha-Gaye do about the isopropyl alcohol in the water bottle?
o: Write 'IPA' on the bottle with a marker and leave it on the bench
Put it in a proper labelled container in the cabinet; scrap the bottle
Move the bottle to a high shelf where nobody is likely to reach it
Pour it down the workshop sink and rinse the bottle for drinking
questions.why: A clear flammable liquid in a drink bottle will sooner or later be drunk or left near a spark. Chemicals stay in proper labelled containers, closed, in the flammables cabinet. A drink bottle that has held a chemical is never used for drinking again.

questions.q: Two batteries are on charge and the extract fan is not running. What is the right action?
o: Open the charger's vents so that the batteries stay cool
Leave them, as two batteries give off very little gas
Move the charger clips to check that they are tight
Stop the charging safely, ventilate, and report the fan
questions.why: Charging lead-acid batteries give off hydrogen, which can build up and explode. Switch the charger off at its supply before touching the clips, since a spark at a terminal can ignite the gas. Ventilate the area and do not charge again until the fan is repaired.

questions.q: Bench 4 has failed for the third week. What should go on the action list this time?
o: 'Tidy bench 4', with a firmer warning to its users
Remove bench 4 from the workshop until further notice
Find the cause with its users and agree a real fix
Take bench 4 off the checklist, since it never passes
questions.why: The same action has failed twice, so the cause has not been touched. Ask the users why: no tool board, a bin too far away, no time allowed? Agree a fix that removes the cause, give it an owner and a date, and check next week whether it worked.

questions.q: The skip was emptied this morning. When should Jermaine have it exchanged?
o: At the end of day 4
At the end of day 6
At the end of day 8
At the end of day 10
questions.why: 8 ÷ 1.25 = 6.4 days, so the skip becomes full during day 7. Booking the exchange for the end of day 6 stops waste piling up beside it. Waiting until day 8 leaves more than a day's waste on the ground.

questions.q: Why must Jermaine refuse the offer to burn the cable offcuts?
o: The copper would melt and run away into the ground
Burning PVC gives off toxic, corrosive fumes, and is illegal
Burnt copper cannot be sold to any scrap dealer in Jamaica
The fire would be too small to burn all the insulation off
questions.why: Burning PVC insulation releases hydrogen chloride and other poisons that harm people nearby and corrode equipment, and open burning of waste breaks environmental rules. The offcuts are kept in the secure scrap container and sold as cable scrap through the firm's procedure.

questions.q: A workshop team writes one daily checklist and gives every bay the same colour-coded waste bins, so that each shift works in the same way. Which 5S step is this?
o: Sort
Shine
Standardise
Sustain
questions.why: Standardise means making the good way the normal way for everyone: the same bins, labels and checklists everywhere. Sort removes what is not needed, Shine is cleaning and inspecting, and Sustain is keeping the system going through inspections and leadership.
